justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing level of CO2 concentrations at Mauna Loa, which has been tracking in the 418–422 ppm range during recent months. For the one-day horizon, I expected very little movement from wherever the current reading sits, since daily fluctuations are modest and dominated by local meteorological noise rather than any meaningful change in atmospheric composition. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher to reflect the persistent long-term upward trend of roughly 2–2.5 ppm per year, while also acknowledging that weekly averages can smooth out some of the day-to-day variability. The one-month estimate continued that trajectory, applying a proportional share of the annual trend and accounting for any seasonal signal — CO2 typically peaks in May and begins declining through Northern Hemisphere summer as vegetation draws carbon down, so the direction of seasonal pressure depends heavily on what month we're currently in.

The confidence interval widths reflect distinctly different sources of uncertainty at each horizon. At one day, the dominant noise comes from wind patterns, local vegetation effects, and measurement conditions at Mauna Loa itself, keeping the range relatively tight. At one week, weather systems and short-term variability in regional carbon fluxes widen the plausible range meaningfully. At one month, the uncertainty compounds further because we are essentially integrating over multiple weather regimes, and the seasonal cycle can either add to or subtract from the trend depending on timing, creating a much wider envelope of plausible outcomes.

There are several specific risks that could push readings outside my stated intervals. On the high side, an anomalously warm or dry period could suppress vegetation uptake, or unusual transport of air masses with elevated CO2 could temporarily inflate readings. A significant El Niño-related drought reducing tropical forest carbon uptake could also push concentrations higher. On the low side, unusually vigorous Northern Hemisphere growing-season drawdown or a persistent flow of cleaner Southern Ocean air could pull readings below the lower bound. Instrument calibration issues or data gaps at Mauna Loa, while rare, represent a tail risk that would affect reported values rather than true atmospheric concentrations. Over the one-month horizon in particular, these compounding factors make the tails of the distribution fatter than the symmetric interval I reported might imply.
